study.title: Songs 7 - Celebrated beauty and invitation to communion
study.overview: This chapter continues the poetic language of love between the beloved and the beloved. In the first verses, the beauty of the woman is described in an increasing way, from walking to the traces of the face and to the whole presence. Then the speech passes from contemplation to reciprocity: she claims to belong to the beloved and calls him to go out with her into the field and for the vineyards. The chapter ends with the image of perfume, saved fruits and shared desire, suggesting joyful affection, abundance and expectation of encounter. The notes available highlight that the sequence of praise goes from the bottom up, which some images can be read as clothes, ornaments or parts of the body, and that the reference to the mandra and fruits points to the pleasure and availability of goods stored for the beloved.

outline.title: Praise of the beauty of the beloved
outline.explanation: The beloved describes the woman in a detailed and progressive manner: feet, legs, womb, breasts, neck, eyes and nose. The intention of the poem is to celebrate his beauty with noble and impressive comparisons, as if it were of royal and harmonious stature.

outline.title: From admiration to the voice that delights
outline.explanation: The description continues with the head, hair and height of the beloved, culminating in the statement that his speech is like excellent wine. The image communicates charm, attraction and the effect of his presence on the beloved and on those who hear it.

outline.title: Beshousing, invitation and saved fruits
outline.explanation: The beloved responds with the language of affective covenant: it belongs to the beloved and desires it. Then he calls him to go out to the field and to the vineyards, and it contains with perfume, mandragons and new and old fruits kept for it, signaling abundance and prepared communion.

study.context: The chapter moves within a loving poetry full of rural, domestic and bodily metaphors. The notes provided mention mandrágoras as plants associated with the Near East and cite tanks and towers linked to known places in the text, such as Hesbom and Lebanon. Still, the main focus is not historical reconstruction, but the imagery force of the poem and reciprocity among lovers.
study.theology: Under an evangelical reading, the chapter celebrates human love as a good gift, marked by beauty, desire, joy and exclusivity. Language is not accidentally erotic; it is poetic and full of admiration, suggesting that conjugal love can involve legitimate pleasure without shame. At the same time, the statement was made up of my beloved, and he desires me to express mutual belonging, not violent possession. The chapter also values the speech that builds and pleases, because the voice of the beloved is compared to good wine. For the Christian faith, this can be read as an invitation to consider faithful love, celebrated with delicacy, reciprocity and generosity, as something that honors the Creator.

scholarViews.insight: The note understands the "mandrágoras" as associated with the Near East and as an image linked to the desire; it also observes the game of words between "mandrágoras" and "my beloved," and sees the "new and old fruit" as pleasures already lived and others still to experience.

The note understands the expression of the new and old fruits as a reference to all sorts of pleasant things, preserved for the beloved; it also highlights that the literal meaning is covered by metaphors and asks the reader caution in the interpretation.

questions: What elements of the language of this chapter show that love here is celebrated with joy, reverence and reciprocity?
How can the affirmation of belonging in 7.10 guide a biblical vision of loving commitment and fidelity?
How does the image of the voice how good wine help to think words that strengthen and please within Christian marriage or dating?
study.practice: Read this chapter as an invitation to gratitude for the beauty of faithful love. If you are married, seek to express concrete admiration to your spouse, not only by appearance, but also by character and presence. If you are unmarried, reflect on how language, desire and commitment must walk together under the wisdom of God. In any state of life, practice words that honor, not that they object; that they celebrate, not to use; that they keep, not to exploit.
study.uncertainty: Some metaphors of the chapter are debated in the notes, especially the descriptions of the belly, the fruits and the mandragons. The sources differ between more body readings and readings more alluding to clothing, ornaments and marital pleasure. It is also not possible to safely determine, only with these notes, how much of the poem should be read literally and how symbolically.
